ledger.note: 1565: Legazpi's first conquests. 'successfully incorporated into Spain's empire Cebu, Samar, Mazaua, Leyte, and Bohol, before conquering Manila.' The page gives no year for this sentence, only the order (before Manila, 1570-1571); 1565 is the researcher's bridge and the page is silent.

region.text: San Miguel, Cebu, the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines

ledger.note: 1565: Legazpi plants the first Spanish settlement of the Philippines at Cebu. 'Legazpi colonizes Cebu: 27 April 1565' (infobox); 'established the first Spanish settlement in the Philippines in 1565', at what is now San Miguel, Cebu. The Spanish colonization page has him 'arriving off Cebu on February 13, 1565, conquering it despite Cebuano opposition'.

1569: Legazpi moves the Spanish headquarters from Cebu to Panay. 'in 1569 Legazpi transferred to Panay and founded a second settlement'; the Captaincy page adds that the move followed a Portuguese attack on Cebu.
1571: Manila becomes the capital. East Indies infobox: 'Manila from 1571 to 1898'. The Captaincy text dates the move to 1595 (disagreement).

1571: the Spaniards take Maynila and rename it Manila. 'the Spaniards captured Maynila and renamed it Manila'. The Spanish colonization page dates the conquest to 1570: 'In 1570, Martín de Goiti ... conquered Maynila'.

minus.text: the Cordillera highlands of Luzon, which 'remained outside Spanish control until the early 19th century'

ledger.note: 1571: Luzon's lowlands. 'The conquest of Luzon was planned, and launched on 8 May 1570'; Goiti and Salcedo 'conquered Luzon's northern region'. The page gives no year for the end of the campaign: 1571 is the researcher's bridge and the page is silent on the extent. The Cordillera highlands are left out ('remained outside Spanish control until the early 19th century', East Indies page).

1574: the Philippines become a captaincy general. 'the Captaincy General of the Philippines was created as a dependency of the Viceroyalty of New Spain' (also the East Indies page). Governed from Mexico until 1821, when it passed to Madrid. The Captaincy infobox itself gives 'Spanish conquest: 27 April 1565'.

1574: Palau enters the East Indies timeline. The page's timeline gives 'Palau as 1574-1899' and says Palau 'was not governed by Spanish missions until the early 19th century': a nominal claim, one grid cell.

region.text: the Cagayan settlement and its valley

ledger.note: 1582: Cagayan subjugated. 'When the Spanish arrived in the area, they subjugated the settlement, resulting in the 1582 Cagayan battles.'

1626: a Spanish post in northern Taiwan (Spanish Formosa). The East Indies timeline gives Taiwan 1626-1642; its infobox says Spain held the area from 1575 until the Dutch invasion in 1646 (the page disagrees with itself). The extent is the researcher's reading: a 40 km circle at Keelung.

1635: the Zamboanga fort. 'The Spanish built a fort called Real Fuerza de San Jose in Zamboanga under Captain Juan de Chavez in 1635' (construction began 23 June). The East Indies page says Zamboanga was 'taken from the Sultanate of Sulu'.
1642: Spanish Formosa lost to the Dutch. 'Loss of Spanish Formosa to the Dutch: 26 August 1642' (infobox); the infobox elsewhere says Spain held the area 'until the Dutch invasion in 1646'.

1663: Zamboanga abandoned. 'Bobadilla, governor of Zamboanga, was ordered to evacuate Zamboanga, which was done in January 1663.' The page does not say who took the ground; the Moro sultanates are the context.

1668: Guam. 'In 1668, Blessed Diego Luis de San Vitores established the first mission on Guam'; the timeline lists the Marianas as 1667-1898. The Captaincy page records that Legazpi 'arrived in Umatac in 1565 and claimed the island of Guam for Spain'.
1686: the Carolines enter the timeline. 'the Carolines as 1686-1899'; the page adds that the Carolines were not governed by Spanish missions until the early 19th century, so this is a nominal claim.

1718: Zamboanga held again. 'The Spanish ordered the Zamboanga fort rebuilt in 1712 and finished it in 1718, when the present fort, with four bastions, was built.' The page does not date the return; the completion year is used.

1724: Basilan ceded. 'In 1724, the Jolo sultan made a treaty of peace with the Spaniards, ceding the island of Basilan.' A fort was erected on Basilan in 1842; the Sulu dossier's page has Sulu giving up Basilan in 1762.

1762: the British take Manila. 'In October 1762, a British expeditionary force captured Manila and occupied it for twenty months.' The Spanish colonization page adds that the British 'were unable to extend their conquest outside of Manila'.
1764: Manila returned. Under the 1763 Treaty of Paris the territories went back to Spain, 'occurring in April 1764'.
1849: the Davao settlement. 'Jose Oyanguren, who, in 1849, took the fort of Hijo' founded the Davao settlement; 'the Davao country was ceded to the Spaniards by the Sultan of Mindanao' (no year).

region.text: the Sultanate of Sulu, whose Sultan 'acknowledged the sovereignty of Spain'

ledger.note: 1851: the Sultan of Jolo acknowledges Spanish sovereignty on paper. 'This treaty was dated and signed April 19, 1851'; the same page also has the Spanish flag raised at Jolo 'In April 1850' (the page disagrees with itself). The sultanate stayed self-governing until the 1876 expedition.

1872: Palawan. After the 1870 raid, 'Two years later a garrison of native troops was placed at Puerto Princesa'; a garrison at Balabac was attacked in 1874. Counterpart 'nobody': the Sulu and Brunei dossiers date earlier cessions of Palawan (1705, 1842) from other pages.
1876: the treaty relation breaks. 'an extensive expedition was planned against the Sultan by the captain-general in 1876.'
1876: Spain moves on Jolo. 'an extensive expedition was planned against the Sultan by the captain-general in 1876'; the page gives no separate year for the capture of Jolo.
1878: Sulu submits. 'the treaty of the Sultan of Jolo and his datus submitting to Spain, signed at Licup (Jolo) July 22, 1878.'

region.text: the Sulu archipelago under the Sultan of Jolo

ledger.note: 1878: Sulu is again a Spanish dependency from the treaty of 22 July 1878. The same page adds the Madrid protocol of 7 March 1885, by which Spain gave up any claim to the land held by the British North Borneo Company.

1896: the Philippine Revolution begins. 'Philippine Revolution: 23 August 1896' (infobox). The page does not name the first battlefields; Luzon is the researcher's reading, as in the Spanish Empire dossier.
1898: the government leaves Manila for Iloilo after the American capture of Manila. The infobox gives 'Iloilo from 13 August to 10 December 1898'.

region.text: the Philippines 'including the islands within a specified line', and Guam

ledger.note: 1898: the Philippines and Guam pass to the United States. The Treaty of Paris 'was signed by Spain and the United States on December 10, 1898'; it 'came into effect on April 11, 1899'; the Philippine cession carried 'a compensation of $20 million'. The East Indies infobox: 'United States annexation of the Philippines and Guam: 10 December 1898'.

1898: the revolution ends for Spain. Declaration of independence 12 June 1898, Battle of Manila 13 August 1898, annexation by the United States 10 December 1898 (infobox); the Spanish colonization page: 'Filipino forces had liberated much of the country from the Spanish'.
1898: Spain's claim over Sulu ends with the cession of the Philippines (Treaty of Paris, 10 December 1898). The page does not mention Sulu; the end of the relation is the researcher's reading.

1899: the last islands sold. 'Spain later sold other smaller islands to Germany in the German-Spanish Treaty of 1899'; the infobox: 'Sale of the remaining islands to Germany: 12 February 1899'. The page does not list the islands (Marianas without Guam, Carolines, Palau is the researcher's reading); the Treaty of Washington of 7 November 1900 later named Cagayan Sulu and Sibutu (Treaty of Paris page).

1899: the Spanish East Indies end. With the Philippines and Guam gone in December 1898 and the remaining islands sold on 12 February 1899, nothing is left; the Captaincy infobox gives 'Withdrawal of Spanish forces: 3 June 1899' and the East Indies page 'remaining islands ceded to the United States: 23 March 1901' (Treaty of Washington).

wars.name: Spanish-Moro conflict
wars.outcome: The Spaniards held Zamboanga (1635-1663, from 1718), received Basilan (1724), Davao (1849) and Sulu's submission (22 July 1878), and fought for Cotabato and Lanao to the 1890s; 'Moro resistance against Spanish colonial authorities continue until the 1898 US capture of the Philippines.'
wars.note: Start year is the first dated event read (Zamboanga fort 1635); the page's own start year was not read.

wars.name: British occupation of Manila
wars.outcome: Manila occupied October 1762 for twenty months; returned in April 1764 under the 1763 Treaty of Paris; the British 'were unable to extend their conquest outside of Manila'.

wars.name: Dutch-Spanish naval actions in the Philippines
wars.outcome: Naval actions in 1610, 1617 and 1624 and the five Battles of La Naval de Manila in 1646; the page records no territorial change.

wars.name: Philippine Revolution
wars.outcome: Revolution from 23 August 1896; independence declared 12 June 1898; by 1898 'Filipino forces had liberated much of the country' (Spanish colonization page) and Spain ceded the islands to the United States.

wars.name: Spanish-American War (Philippine theatre)
wars.outcome: Battle of Manila 13 August 1898; Treaty of Paris signed 10 December 1898; Spain ceded the Philippines and Guam for $20 million.
wars.note: Dated from the Captaincy page's infobox for the battle.

certainty.note: Spanish control was a string of settlements and forts; the Cordillera, most of Mindanao and Sulu stayed outside. Every outline here is approximate.
The Jolo treaty of 22 July 1878 and the Madrid protocol of 7 March 1885 fix Sulu and North Borneo on paper only; Mindanao's interior was 'nominally under Spanish control'.
The Treaty of Paris fixed a specified line round the archipelago; the German sale of 12 February 1899 named islands, not a line.

notes:
Written 2026-10-20 by the se-03-x additions batch: a state Cliopatria lacks (cliopatria_names empty, every keyframe new). Five pages opened of a five-page budget. One dossier for the whole Spanish East Indies (Philippines, Marianas, Carolines, Palau, and Spanish Formosa 1626-1642) under the Captaincy General's life, 1565 to 12 February 1899; type colony, its tint is the Spanish Empire's (spanish-empire dossier, am-06). The Spanish Empire dossier also carries the Philippine gains; the renderer should draw this colony as the vassal tint of the metropole and not twice.
Unsettled: (1) the pages date the capital move to Manila differently (1571 East Indies infobox, 1595 Captaincy text); the capital at Panay 1569-1570 has no named town (Oton is the researcher's coordinate). (2) The pages give no territory for the Visayan conquest after Cebu (confidence 1), for Luzon's north, Palawan before 1872, Mindanao outside the forts, the Cordillera after the early 19th century, or the Carolines and Palau (page: not governed until the early 19th century). The shapes are the researcher's readings of named provinces. (3) The Moro conflict page is internally inconsistent on Jolo (flag raised April 1850, treaty April 19, 1851) and dates Basilan's cession to 1724 while the Sulu dossier's page says 1762. (4) Zamboanga's counterpart is sultanate-of-sulu on the East Indies page's wording; the Moro page names no state. (5) The Treaty of Paris page does not mention the Philippine Revolution or Sulu; the 1898 vassal_end for Sulu is a reading. (6) Cliopatria's Maynila row is placed in the Ryukyus (seed centroid 127.8E 26.7N) and is not used. (7) Spanish Formosa dates conflict on the page (1626-1642 timeline, until 1646 infobox). (8) Governors-general: the pages give no list, so identity.rulers is omitted.
Needs a dossier: first-philippine-republic (1898-1901). Gazetteer: nothing missing; all places and regions resolved by name.
